meta.subtitle: Revenue growth picked up to 36% in the second quarter, but the shares already trade above the Street's average target

analystSentiment.commentary:
Cloudflare's second quarter of 2026 was strong at the top line and noisy below it. Revenue rose {+ 36% year over year +} to $696.1 million, and Current RPO grew 35%. The GAAP loss from operations widened to {- $205.7 million -}, and the company's own disclosures point to restructuring charges from its May 2026 workforce reduction (see Financials). On the company's non-GAAP measure, income from operations was $96.1 million.

Our concern is the price, not the business. At $357.95 the shares sit close to their 52-week high and above the consensus target of $338.71, and they trade at 283.4x consensus earnings for this year. That multiple leaves little room for a slower quarter.

We rate the shares HOLD with a $330–$380 target range. The call sits nearer the SELL line than the BUY line, and the Valuation section argues the deciding split.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Cloudflare, Inc. operates a global network that delivers security, performance and reliability services to businesses of all sizes, from individual developers to large enterprises. The network has a presence in more than 335 cities and over 125 countries. Its products span application security, application performance, Zero Trust and network services, developer products and consumer offerings, and the company reports them as a single segment.

The company was incorporated in 2009 and is headquartered in San Francisco, California; its fiscal year ends December 31. Fiscal 2025 revenue was $2,167.9 million, up 29.8%. Revenue comes mainly from subscriptions, sold under contracts to larger customers and through the website to pay-as-you-go customers, with a free tier alongside (see Business and moat). Cloudflare earns a profit on its non-GAAP measure but reports losses under GAAP.

Its Class A common stock is listed on the NYSE. A second class of shares, Class B, carries 10 votes per share and gives insiders as a group a majority of the votes (see Management).

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body:
Cloudflare is a fast-growing network business that generates cash but still reports GAAP losses. The case for owning it rests on growth: revenue growth has picked up in 2026, Current RPO is growing at a similar pace, and the company's guidance points to further sequential gains (see Growth). The case against rests on price. The shares trade at forward multiples that hold only if growth stays near today's rate for years (see Valuation).

That leaves the payoff lopsided. Our Bull case needs investors to keep paying today's multiple a year from now. Our Bear case needs only a slowdown and a re-rating toward prices the stock has seen within the last 52 weeks. We therefore neither chase the momentum nor bet against a business that is executing.

catalysts: Third-quarter results against the August 6, 2026 guide of $736.0 to $737.0 million in revenue and $129.0 to $130.0 million in non-GAAP income from operations (see Growth).
Evidence that the agentic AI-first operating model and the May 2026 workforce reduction lift margins, a benefit the company says may come late or not at all (see Growth).
Current RPO growth of 35% converting into revenue in support of the fiscal 2026 revenue guide of $2,864.0 to $2,870.0 million (see Growth).
Revenue or usage figures that back management's view that AI agents are reshaping Internet traffic in Cloudflare's favor (see Growth).
risks: The shares price in years of growth near today's rate, so a slowdown would likely hit the multiple as well as earnings (see Valuation).
Gross margin fell in fiscal 2025 and again in the second quarter, and the excerpts give no reason (see Financials and Risks).
The move to an agentic AI-first operating model could disrupt operations or the network during the transition (see Risks).
Insiders as a group hold a majority of the votes through Class B stock while owning a small minority of the shares (see Management).
Macro pressure that the company says lengthened sales cycles and raised churn in past periods could recur (see Risks).

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Annual revenue growth slowed from +48.6% in FY22 to +28.8% in FY24, then steadied at +29.8% in fiscal 2025; the 2026 pickup is covered under Growth. Profitability has not kept pace with the top line.

Gross margin is moving the wrong way. GAAP gross margin was {- 74.5% -} in fiscal 2025, down from 77.3% in fiscal 2024, and {- 71.8% -} in the second quarter of 2026, down from 74.9% a year earlier. The non-GAAP gross margin fell by a similar amount year over year, to 73.1% from 76.3%. We have no explanation for the decline in the excerpts and do not supply one, but a sustained slide would undercut the cost advantage the company claims.

The GAAP loss from operations widened to $205.7 million, or 29.6% of revenue, from $67.3 million, or 13.1%, in the second quarter of 2025. The company's account points to restructuring: the income statement carries a new "Restructuring and other charges" line, absent a year earlier, and the 10-Q says the May 2026 workforce reduction "has resulted in severance and other restructuring charges." That line alone is larger than the year-over-year increase in the operating loss, so the underlying GAAP trend is better than the headline. GAAP net loss was $170.0 million, or $0.48 per share, against $50.4 million, or $0.15. The trailing-twelve-month GAAP operating margin of -14.1% carries these charges.

On the company's non-GAAP basis, income from operations rose to {+ $96.1 million +} from $72.3 million, but the margin slipped to {- 13.8% -} from 14.1%. Non-GAAP net income per diluted share rose to $0.29 from $0.21. Besides the restructuring line, the main gap between GAAP and non-GAAP results is stock-based compensation and related payroll taxes, which in the quarter were larger than non-GAAP operating income but grew far more slowly than revenue. Revenue is compounding, but neither measure of operating margin has yet shown the leverage the valuation assumes.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary:
The balance sheet is not a constraint. At the end of fiscal 2025, cash and short-term investments of $4.1B exceeded total debt of $3.3B. Both rose sharply during the year, from $1.9B and $1.3B, which suggests much of the new borrowing was kept as liquidity. The cash cost of the debt looks small: in the second quarter of 2026, interest income was many times interest expense, and most of interest expense was amortization of debt issuance costs.

The vendor's Net Debt row, $2.3B for fiscal 2025, subtracts only cash and cash equivalents from total debt and leaves out the investment securities counted in cash and short-term investments, so it overstates net debt. On the broader measure, Cloudflare holds more cash and investments than debt. At June 30, 2026, the company reported cash, cash equivalents, and available-for-sale securities of $4,162.8 million; we have no debt figure for that date, so the year-end comparison is the cleanest. The vendor's net debt/EBITDA of -12.4x and interest coverage of -30.9x are negative only because EBITDA and operating income are negative, and we do not use them.

The current ratio has fallen every year, from 6.78 in FY21 to 1.98 in FY25, and stands at 1.82 on a trailing basis. It remains above one, so short-term obligations are covered, but the cushion is much thinner than it was. Total equity was $1.5B at the end of fiscal 2025. For a company that generates operating cash, liquidity is ample, and we see no financing risk within our horizon.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
The Facts table and the company disagree on free cash flow because they define it differently. The Facts table deducts only capital expenditure from operating cash flow, which gives $287.5M for fiscal 2025. The company's own measure also deducts capitalized internal-use software and comes out lower. We use the company's figures throughout, because they match the quarterly figures in its earnings release.

Cash generation is rising. Fiscal 2025 operating cash flow was $603.1 million, up from $380.4 million, and free cash flow was $260.6 million, or 12.0% of revenue, up from $166.9 million, or 10.0%. In the second quarter of 2026, operating cash flow was $117.6 million against $99.8 million a year earlier, and free cash flow was {+ $56.4 million +}, or 8% of revenue, against $33.3 million, or 6%.

Network spending is the swing factor. Capital expenditure rose to $315.6M in fiscal 2025 from the prior year in the Facts table. The MD&A says the company intends "to continue to make substantial investments in our global network infrastructure," including servers with storage capabilities and "servers with graphics processing units (GPUs) to support our AI-related developer platform products." We read that as heavy spending ahead.

Operating cash flow also benefits from stock-based pay, which costs no cash but shows up as dilution (see Capital allocation). Free cash flow is real and growing, but it understates the full cost of running the business, and the planned network build will absorb part of any gains.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
GAAP multiples are not usable. The trailing P/E of -617.2x and EV/EBITDA of -999.3x are negative because trailing GAAP earnings and EBITDA are negative.

The forward multiples need a closer look. The vendor labels 283.4x a next-twelve-months P/E, but it lines up with FY26E consensus EPS of $1.26 rather than FY27E's $1.68, so in practice it is a current-year multiple. On FY27E, the shares trade at about 213.6x. Both multiples rest on non-GAAP earnings: that FY26E figure sits at the top of the company's guide for non-GAAP net income per share (see Growth), while GAAP results are losses. On trailing-twelve-month revenue the shares trade at 50.7x, and the vendor's trailing free cash flow yield is 0.3%. We have no peer set in this pack, so we judge these levels on their own: they price in years of growth near today's rate.

The Street is more cautious than its ratings. Of 34 analysts, 23 rate the stock Buy, 8 Hold and 3 Sell, yet the consensus target of $338.71 is 5.4% below the price, and the median target of $355.00 is also below it. Targets range from $160.00 to $405.00, and the mean sits below the median, so the low end of the range pulls the average down.

The price has moved sharply. The shares trade at $357.95, close to the 52-week high of $370.35 and far above the 52-week low of $158.83, and no headline or document in this pack explains the move. The price has run past both the mean and the median target, so at these multiples the stock needs results to keep improving just to hold its level.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Revenue growth holds at or above the second quarter's pace, gross margin steadies and the new operating model lifts margins. A year from now, investors still pay today's 283.4x current-year multiple, now applied to FY27E consensus EPS of $1.68. That gives $476, above the top of the Street target range at $405.00.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Cloudflare meets its fiscal 2026 guidance and FY27E consensus EPS, but the multiple on current-year earnings compresses to about today's 213.6x FY27E level as the year rolls forward. Earnings growth is absorbed by de-rating, and the price ends at the Street median target of $355.00.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Revenue growth slows to or below fiscal 2025's 29.8%, gross margin keeps falling and the operating-model change disappoints, so FY27 EPS stalls near the FY26E consensus of $1.26. The multiple on that EPS falls by more than half from today's current-year level, taking the price to the Street low target of $160.00, next to the 52-week low of $158.83.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
Base gets 65%. The fiscal 2026 guide from August 6, 2026 covers two remaining quarters, and Current RPO growth supports it, so we expect the year to land in range and FY27E consensus to hold. What we do not expect is for the multiple to hold. Our Base assumes the multiple on current-year earnings gives back about as much as earnings add as the year rolls forward. We anchor it to the Street median target rather than the mean because the mean is pulled down by the low end of the range, which our Bear already captures.

Bull gets 20%. It needs growth to stay at or above the second quarter's pace and investors to keep paying today's multiple. The growth evidence supports it; the falling gross margin and the dip in non-GAAP operating margin cut against it. The Bull sits above the top of the Street target range. We do not cap it there, because the price already sits above the consensus target, so targets have not acted as a ceiling.

Bear gets 15%, on its own merits. It needs two things at once: a slowdown that holds FY27 EPS near this year's level, and a multiple that falls by more than half. The re-rating alone is plausible, since the stock traded near the Bear price within the last 52 weeks. The slowdown is less likely within twelve months, because Current RPO and the third-quarter guide point the other way and the balance sheet makes forced funding unlikely. Both together are a real but minority outcome.

This is a close call between HOLD and SELL. Swapping the Bull and Bear weights, or anchoring Base to the mean target instead of the median, would each push the weighted value below the SELL line. We keep the split above because the near-term growth evidence is stronger than the evidence for a collapse. The derived label is HOLD, and that is our call.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Cloudflare reports one segment, so all of fiscal 2025 revenue sits in it. Revenue comes mainly from subscriptions to the network and its products. Contracted customers on the Enterprise subscription plan sign contracts that typically range from one to three years, usually billed monthly or annually, and some larger customers commit to a "pool of funds" they can spend across products during the term. Pay-as-you-go customers buy Pro and Business plans through the website, Zero Trust and network services products sell per seat, and developer products are metered by requests and execution time. A free tier sits alongside. The company does not break out revenue by product, so we cannot tell which offering drives the acceleration; the mix of committed contracts and usage-based plans gives revenue a contracted base with some sensitivity to usage.

moatFactors.name: Network cost position
moatFactors.body: The company says agreements with ISPs let it place equipment in their data centers, which "drives down our bandwidth and co-location expenses," and that its network lets it introduce new products "at low marginal cost." GAAP gross margin between 74.5% and 77.6% across the five fiscal years in the Facts table is consistent with that claim. The recent slide in gross margin (see Financials) is the counter-evidence: the edge exists, but it is not widening.

moatFactors.name: Platform breadth and expansion
moatFactors.body: Customer relationships "often start with servicing a portion of their overall needs and expand over time," and the company sees upsell as customers "seek to consolidate onto one infrastructure platform." Larger customers can commit to a "pool of funds" that they spend across products. These features raise the cost of leaving once several products are in use. No measure of expansion is disclosed in the excerpts, so we rate this factor on structure rather than data.

moatFactors.name: Free and self-serve funnel
moatFactors.body: Free customers "create scale, serve as efficient brand marketing," and expose the network to diverse traffic and threats, per the MD&A. The pay-as-you-go offering has let the company acquire a large portion of its paying customers "at significantly lower customer acquisition costs than our other product offerings." The value depends on conversion, and the company lists its ability to "convert free customers to paying customers" among the factors that could affect results. We count it as a real distribution edge.

moatFactors.name: Developer and AI platform
moatFactors.body: The MD&A says customers increasingly build applications on the network, including ones "enhanced with artificial intelligence," and the company is adding GPU servers for AI-related developer products. Applications built on the network would be harder to move than services bought on top of it. The AI case is unquantified (see Growth), so this factor is potential rather than proven.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat NARROW. The factors above are real, but they have not yet shown up in profits: the company still reports GAAP losses, and operating margins have not expanded (see Financials). Revenue growth of at least 28.8% in each of the last four fiscal years shows durable demand, yet growth alone does not prove pricing power or a lasting cost edge. A WIDE rating would need GAAP profits and stable gross margin. We have no peer data in this pack, so we cannot rank the network against others. The test of durability is whether the network keeps its cost position as the company adds GPU and storage capacity, and gross margin over the next few quarters will show it.

points: Revenue growth has turned up. Second-quarter revenue grew {+ 36% +} year over year to $696.1 million, faster than any full fiscal year since FY22's +48.6%, and the CEO described revenue as "accelerating." He also pointed to growth in total paying customers, large customers and developers, but the release gives no counts. One quarter is not a trend, but the direction is right.

Current RPO supports the near term. Current RPO grew 35% year over year in the second quarter, close to the revenue growth rate. It is not a revenue guarantee: the MD&A notes that "pool of funds" customers need not spend any specific amount in a given month, quarter or year of the subscription period, so recognized revenue can lag commitments. On balance, it makes a sharp slowdown in the next few quarters less likely.

Guidance points to sequential gains. On August 6, 2026, the company guided third-quarter revenue to $736.0 to $737.0 million and non-GAAP income from operations to $129.0 to $130.0 million, above the second quarter's $96.1 million, with non-GAAP net income per share of $0.34. For fiscal 2026 it guided revenue to $2,864.0 to $2,870.0 million non-GAAP income from operations to $443.0 to $445.0 million and non-GAAP net income per share to $1.25 to $1.26. The company says a GAAP reconciliation of this guidance is not available "without unreasonable effort," so the GAAP path stays unclear.

The AI argument is large but unquantified. The CEO says the web's shift "to AI answer engines and agent-driven commerce" amounts to "a fundamental rewrite of the Internet for machine-to-machine traffic," and that Cloudflare is building "the infrastructure, controls, developer tools, and payment rails for the Agentic Internet." His claim that "no company is better positioned than Cloudflare" is an assertion, and the release attaches no revenue to it. We treat AI as an option on the platform, not an input to our numbers.

The operating-model change is the margin lever. The company is moving to "an agentic AI-first operating model" and says the workforce reduction announced in May 2026 "has been substantially completed." It also says it "may not realize the expected operating efficiencies, cost savings, or other expected benefits of these changes within the expected timeframe, if at all." Savings should show first in non-GAAP operating margin, the measure that slipped in the second quarter (see Financials).

management.leadership:
Cloudflare is founder-led. According to the proxy statement filed in June 2026, Matthew Prince is Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer and Michelle Zatlyn is Co-Founder and President, and both serve as Co-Chair of the Board of Directors; Ms. Zatlyn was appointed Co-Chair on February 5, 2025. Thomas Seifert is Chief Financial Officer. The legal function changed hands this year. Douglas Kramer stepped down as Chief Legal Officer effective March 31, 2026, and Alissa Starzak, previously Deputy Chief Legal Officer and Global Head of Public Policy, became Chief Legal Officer and Secretary on April 1, 2026. Mr. Kramer stayed on as Senior Advisor at an annual base salary of $100,000 and keeps vesting his previously unvested RSU awards and Performance Options.

Founder leadership gives continuity, and the team's main decision this year is the shift to an agentic AI-first operating model (see Growth and Risks). We judge leadership on whether that shift delivers margin without slowing growth, and the evidence is not in yet.
management.capitalAllocation:
Capital goes back into the business. Cloudflare paid no dividend and repurchased no stock in fiscal 2025. The MD&A names its investment priorities as product development, the global network and the sales force, particularly for contracted customers. In fiscal 2025 it also raised debt and largely held the proceeds as liquidity (see Balance sheet). The release footnotes show amortization of acquired intangible assets and acquisition-related expenses in the second quarter, so acquisitions play some role, though no deal is described.

The cost to shareholders comes as dilution rather than cash. The weighted-average share count used for loss per share rose year over year in the second quarter, and stock-based pay is a large expense (see Financials). For its non-GAAP EPS guidance, the company assumes approximately 374 million weighted average shares. Reinvestment is the right call while growth is this strong, but holders should expect continued dilution, not buybacks.
management.governance:
The proxy statement filed in June 2026 describes a board on which all but three directors are independent and which is chaired by two executives. The board determined that every director other than Dr. Graham-Cumming, Mr. Prince and Ms. Zatlyn is independent under NYSE standards, and NYSE rules require independent audit, compensation, and nominating and corporate governance committees, subject to specified exceptions. Mr. Prince and Ms. Zatlyn, the CEO and the President, are both Co-Chairs. The excerpt is cut off before it describes any independent counterweight to the Co-Chairs and before the pay tables, so we cannot assess either. The related-party section, as excerpted, covers the new offer letters for Mr. Kramer and Ms. Starzak.

The larger governance fact is the dual-class structure (see Insider ownership). Combined with executive Co-Chairs, it leaves outside shareholders little formal leverage over strategy, including the operating-model change now under way. That does not rule the stock out, but it argues for a margin of safety the current price does not offer.
management.insiderOwnership:
The proxy's ownership table is as of April 30, 2026, when 319,528,379 Class A shares and 33,937,897 Class B shares were outstanding. Class A carries one vote per share and Class B carries 10, and the two classes vote together on all matters except as the certificate of incorporation or law may require. Mr. Prince beneficially owned 25,693,312 Class B shares, 75.7% of that class, for 39.0% of total voting power. Ms. Zatlyn owned 9,016,720 Class B shares, 25.5% of the class, for 13.4% of the vote. All executive officers and directors as a group (11 persons) held 99.0% of Class B and 52.4% of total voting power.

The economic stake is far smaller than the vote. Class B shares are a small fraction of the share count, and each insider's Class A holding is under one percent of that class. Insiders as a group therefore hold a majority of the votes while owning a small minority of the shares, though no single holder, Mr. Prince included, has a majority on his own. Capital World Investors, by contrast, owns 11.4% of Class A but carries 5.5% of the vote. For outside holders, this means the insider group, voting together, could decide any matter settled by a simple majority while bearing a small part of the economic outcome.

idiosyncratic: Growth slowdown against a full multiple. The 10-Q warns that "our revenue growth rates may slow or decline in the future" and asks investors not to rely on past growth. At the multiples discussed under Valuation, a return to fiscal 2025's growth rate would likely cost the stock a large part of its multiple; that is the path our Bear case describes. Quarterly revenue growth against the second quarter's pace, and Current RPO growth against revenue growth, are the early signals.

Gross-margin erosion. Gross margin fell in fiscal 2025 and again year over year in the second quarter (see Financials). If the slide continues, the cost advantage behind our NARROW moat rating weakens, and operating-margin gains would have to come from operating expenses alone, which puts more weight on the new operating model to deliver.

Operational risk from the transition. The 10-Q says heavier use of AI and automation "could increase the risk of operational disruptions and errors, network interruptions, control failures or other significant events, particularly during transition periods," and that the workforce reduction may hurt morale and lead to "further attrition of key talent." For a company that sells reliability, an outage tied to the transition could cost more in reputation than the savings return. The company also flags possible further costs, including claims by employees or works councils.

Persistent GAAP losses. The company has "incurred net losses in all periods since we began operations," and its accumulated deficit was $1,397.8 million at June 30, 2026. The six-month net loss widened to $192.9 million from $88.9 million, much of it from the second-quarter charges (see Financials). GAAP profit is not in sight on this year's numbers.
risks.systemic: Cloudflare's macro exposure runs through customer budgets and equipment costs. The MD&A says the company has periodically seen longer sales cycles, slower pipeline conversion, higher days sales outstanding, higher churn and slower payment, all of which "may have contributed to a slowdown in our revenue growth from prior periods." It believes "macroeconomic uncertainty could persist through 2026" and that some of these trends "may emerge or recur." Tariffs are a cost risk: the company buys network equipment from suppliers outside the United States and from U.S. suppliers that use foreign components, and says future tariffs "could cause the costs of the equipment we use to operate our global network to increase." Retaliatory measures against U.S. companies add risk for a business that sells worldwide, and the release flags conflicts in Eastern Europe and the Middle East. Finally, a stock at this multiple is exposed to any market-wide fall in what investors will pay for distant earnings. None of these is unique to Cloudflare, but the valuation magnifies their effect on the share price.

body: We rate Cloudflare HOLD with a target range of $330–$380, which brackets our Base value of $355. The second quarter gave no reason to doubt the business, and the share price gives no reason to add to it. Our scenarios put the weighted value slightly below the current price; the rating rule reads that as HOLD, and we agree.

We would turn more positive, and revisit BUY, if gross margin stops falling year over year and non-GAAP operating margin expands year over year while revenue growth holds above fiscal 2025's 29.8%; the third-quarter results will give an early read on the margin half. We would move to SELL if revenue growth falls back below fiscal 2025's rate, if third-quarter revenue misses the guide of $736.0 to $737.0 million, or if the price climbs back to the 52-week high of $370.35 without higher estimates, which on our scenarios would take the expected return past the SELL line.
